title: Stop Weaponizing Miller's Law
intro: Miller studied how much people hold in working memory **once information is gone**. A visible menu requires no memorising, so his finding says nothing about how many items it should have.

learn.title: What Miller actually studied
learn.text:
Miller's 1956 research asked people to repeat information they could **no longer see** — a string of digits, for example.

A dropdown that stays open is a different task entirely: users scan, compare and go back. Labels and grouping decide whether they succeed, not the item count.

try.q: Why doesn't 7 ± 2 apply to an open dropdown?
options: Nothing has to be remembered — the items are visible
Dropdowns scroll, so length doesn't matter
Miller's sample was too small to generalise
Menus are scanned faster than digits are recalled
try.explain: Recall and recognition are different tasks.

learn.title: Two ways it gets weaponised
learn.text:
**As a shortcut.** Nine items become seven, and nobody asks whether the labels are clear or the grouping matches users' mental models.

**As a conversation-ender.** Once a famous study is invoked, questioning the decision sounds like questioning science — so nobody shows that the original was confusing or the new version is better.

try.q: A team cuts a nine-item menu to seven and closes the discussion. What went unexamined?
options: Whether the labels and grouping work
Whether seven is the correct limit
Whether the menu should be a sidebar
Whether the removed items were popular
try.explain: Trimming the count doesn't address the structure, which is what actually decides success.

learn.title: Don't swap 7 for 4
learn.text:
Newer research puts working memory capacity lower than Miller's figure. The answer isn't to cap menus at four instead.

**Real working-memory problems do exist** — a verification code carried between screens, values compared across pages — but those are design flaws to remove, not a rule about list length.

try.q: Which of these genuinely taxes working memory?
options: A code you must carry to the next screen
A visible list of twelve navigation links
A long settings page with section headings
A table of values with a sticky header row
try.explain: The information disappears and must be held in mind.

options: Working memory for information you can't see
The ideal number of items in a menu
How many choices a person will compare
The number of steps users tolerate in a flow
test.explain: It is a memory finding, not an interface rule.

test.q: What decides whether users succeed with a visible menu?
options: Labels and grouping
The number of items
The order the items were added
How many levels deep it goes
test.explain: Scanning is a recognition task; clarity matters more than count.

test.q: Why is citing a famous study as a conversation-ender a problem?
options: Disagreeing starts to sound like questioning science
Famous studies are usually poorly replicated
It takes too long to read the original paper
Stakeholders dislike academic references
test.explain: So nobody shows that the original was confusing or the new version is better.

test.q: Newer research suggests working memory is smaller than Miller said. What follows for menus?
options: Nothing — the finding still isn't about menus
Menus should be capped at four items
Menus should be replaced with search
Items should be shown four at a time
test.explain: Swapping one wrong number for another misses the point.

test.q: A verification code must be carried from one screen to the next. What should you do?
options: Remove the memory demand from the design
Limit the next screen to seven fields
Add a reminder tooltip on the second screen
Accept it — codes are inherently hard to handle
test.explain: Genuine working-memory demands are design flaws to remove.
